newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Racial grievances underlie latest S.African riots.
newsitem.headline: Racial grievances underlie latest S.African riots.

text.p: Bloody riots have highlighted the grievances of South Africa's mixed-race community, oppressed by apartheid and now some feel discriminated against under black rule.

Police told local media that two men and a boy aged seven died on Thursday in the running battles through the streets of coloured, or mixed-race, suburbs of Johannesburg. On Friday police said they were still checking reports of dead but confirmed that scores of people were wounded.
A woman also told newspapers her nephew, a fourth victim, had died in crossfire between police and rioters protesting at what they claim is unfair treatment by black-run city councils.
The riots, among the worst since the end of white minority rule in 1994, died out after council representatives agreed to meet local coloured leaders to hear their complaints.
"The government should take this opportunity -- it will be the last -- to look into the problem of the coloured nation," Basil Douglas, who organised the protests, told Reuters.
"We coloured people were slaves in the 17th century already, and now we are being made slaves again in our own country."
Politicians and commentators of all colours say such claims are outrageous, but the riots showed how deep resentment goes.
Scenes of burning tyres, stone-throwing and police firing rubber bullets were like a flashback to the anti-apartheid past, but this time most of the protesters were coloured, not black.
Coloureds were classed as one of four race groups under apartheid, along with whites, blacks and Asians and were forced into segregated areas like those that saw Thursday's riots.

They are descendants of South Africa's original inhabitants, the yellow-skinned Khoisan (bushmen and hottentots), of Malay slaves and of interracial couples. Many speak Afrikaans, long seen by blacks as the language of oppression.
The white government oppressed all other races under apartheid but treated coloureds and Asians better, causing a source of bitterness among many blacks that persists.
"We had nothing under apartheid when they only looked after the whites. But now the blacks only look after themselves. What must we do?" said one coloured woman at a barricade.
"The government thinks we coloureds benefited from apartheid but we suffered the same oppression as blacks," said local resident Ronald Jacobs.
Douglas said coloureds were now victims of revenge, sackings and discrimination; "We are facing economic ethnic cleansing."
President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress, which has some coloured members, says such claims are absurd.
Political analysts agree there seems to be no intended discrimination, but that coloureds and whites had good arguments to show black-run local councils treated them differently.

Tom Lodge, of Johannesburg's Witwatersrand University, said poor whites had been evicted for not paying rent in the city while blacks who did not pay up under apartheid but who were still not paying in the new South Africa had been left alone.
Such issues were at the core of the protests organised by Douglas' local group, the South Western Joint Civic Association.
The black-oriented Sowetan newspaper said the rioters' grievances were perfectly justified, but lamented the violence.
Apartheid instilled a culture of rent boycotts, guns and street violence that Mandela's government has failed to root out.
In a country still struggling to break out of race-based politics, many coloureds prefer to vote for the once whites-only National Party rather than throw their lot in with the black-led ANC.
The community of some 3.5 million people, eight percent of the population, have no strong political party of their own.
They have so far mobilised around pressure groups like Douglas' association or the anti-drugs vigilante group Pagad in Cape Town, which has also been responsible for street riots.

"The extent of yesterday's unrest shows widespread, deeply felt dissatisfaction which has racial undertones of coloured against black. That is the last thing the country needs now," said the Afrikaans-language Beeld newspaper.
